examiner_view: Family Law is a high-volume, low-difficulty zone: most questions are one-line recall of a section number, a time period, a landmark case or 'which is correct' on a personal-law rule. Numbers (ages, years, months, fractions) are the favourite.

Expect the 8 Family Law questions to spread roughly as: Hindu law (marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption, guardianship, succession, joint family) 3-4; Muslim law 2-3; Christian/Parsi/Special Marriage Act 1; statutes such as Domestic Violence Act, Dowry Prohibition Act, Child Marriage Act, maintenance under BNSS 1-2. This split is an estimate.

The 2 Cyber Law questions almost always come from the IT Act: offences and punishments (S.65-67B, 66C/66D/66F), S.66A strike-down (Shreya Singhal), S.69A, S.79 intermediary safe harbour, definitions, digital signature, adjudication. Add one current-affairs hook: DPDP Act 2023 / Rules 2025, IT Rules 2021 and the 2026 synthetic-content amendment.

Recent-development questions are plausible in both subjects: Shayara Bano and the 2019 Act, Abdul Samad (2024), Shilpa Sailesh (2023), X v Y (2025, S.25 HMA in void marriages), Supriyo (2023), state UCCs (Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Assam), Waqf Amendment Act 2025 interim order, Puttaswamy, DPDP Rules 2025.
Because BNS/BNSS replaced IPC/CrPC from 1 July 2024, a stem may quote either numbering (e.g. S.498A IPC or S.85 BNS; S.125 CrPC or S.144 BNSS). Learn both.

numbers_cheat_sheet.marriage_age: Hindu/SMA/PCMA: groom 21, bride 18. Muslim: puberty (15 presumed) under classical law, but PCMA 2006 prohibits child marriage (conflict in courts).
numbers_cheat_sheet.hma_divorce_periods: Desertion 2 years; not heard of 7 years; no divorce petition within 1 year of marriage (S.14); mutual consent: 1 year separation before petition, 6-month wait (waivable), maximum 18 months; wife's puberty repudiation: married before 15, repudiate before 18.
numbers_cheat_sheet.sapinda: 3 generations on mother's side, 5 on father's side (S.3(f) HMA).
numbers_cheat_sheet.hama_adoption: Adoptee under 15 unless custom; 21-year gap for opposite sex; adopter must not have Hindu son/son's son/son's son's son (for son) or daughter/son's daughter (for daughter).
numbers_cheat_sheet.hmga: Minor = under 18; custody of child under 5 ordinarily with mother; guardian's lease beyond 5 years needs court permission.
numbers_cheat_sheet.muslim: Iddat: 3 menstrual courses/3 months (divorce), 4 months 10 days (widow), till delivery if pregnant. Will: 1/3 without heirs' consent. Hanafi minimum mahr: 10 dirhams. Pre-emption: 3 demands.
numbers_cheat_sheet.dmma_1939_s2: Whereabouts unknown 4 years; no maintenance 2 years; husband's imprisonment 7 years; failure of marital obligations 3 years; insanity 2 years; puberty option: married before 15, repudiate before 18 (not consummated).
numbers_cheat_sheet.dowry: S.3 Dowry Act: min 5 years + fine min Rs 15,000 or value of dowry; S.4 demand: 6 months-2 years; dowry death: 7 years to life; S.498A/BNS 85: up to 3 years + fine; dowry to be handed to woman within 3 months (S.6).
numbers_cheat_sheet.dv_act: Disposal in 60 days; breach of protection order: up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 20,000 or both; appeal to Sessions Court in 30 days.
numbers_cheat_sheet.pcma_2006: Annulment petition within 2 years of attaining majority; adult male marrying child: up to 2 years RI or fine up to Rs 1 lakh; offences cognizable and non-bailable.
numbers_cheat_sheet.sma_1954: 30-day public notice; 30 days for objections; marry within 3 months of notice; mutual consent divorce after 1 year separation.
numbers_cheat_sheet.it_act: IT Act in force 17 Oct 2000; 2008 amendment in force 27 Oct 2009; S.66A struck down 24 Mar 2015; S.67: 3 years + Rs 5 lakh (first), 5 years + Rs 10 lakh (repeat); S.67A/67B: 5 years + Rs 10 lakh (first), 7 years + Rs 10 lakh (repeat); S.66F: life; S.69/69A: up to 7 years + fine; S.70: up to 10 years; S.72: 2 years/Rs 1 lakh; S.72A: 3 years/Rs 5 lakh.
numbers_cheat_sheet.dpdp: Act assented 11 Aug 2023; Rules notified 13 Nov 2025; child = under 18; maximum penalty Rs 250 crore; Board plus appeal to TDSAT; full obligations phased to about 12 May 2027.

sections.title: Family Law

background.summary: Family Law in India is personal-law based. Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs) are governed by codified statutes of 1955-56 (HMA, HSA, HMGA, HAMA); Muslims by uncodified Shariat plus the Shariat Application Act 1937, DMMA 1939, the 1986 Act and the 2019 Act; Christians by the Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872, Divorce Act 1869 and Indian Succession Act 1925; Parsis by the 1936 Act; inter-faith couples by the Special Marriage Act 1954. Secular overlays include S.144 BNSS (maintenance), DV Act 2005, Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, PCMA 2006, JJ Act 2015 and the Family Courts Act 1984. The 2023-2026 trend is towards gender-just reading (Shayara Bano, Abdul Samad, X v Y, Vineeta Sharma), personal-law reform (state UCCs, Waqf amendment) and procedural reform (Shilpa Sailesh, Rajnesh v Neha).
background.approach: For each personal law, learn (1) the governing Act, (2) marriage conditions, (3) divorce modes and periods, (4) maintenance, (5) guardianship/adoption, (6) succession. Then compare across laws using the personal_law_comparison table.

topics.title: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 - Validity of Marriage, Void and Voidable Marriages, Children
topics.summary: Know the five conditions of S.5, which breach makes a marriage void (S.11), voidable (S.12) or only punishable, the role of ceremonies and registration, and S.16 legitimacy of children.
key_points: Applicability (S.2): Hindus by religion in any form (including Virashaiva, Lingayat, Brahmo, Prarthana, Arya Samaj), Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, and any domiciled person who is not Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew. Does not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless the Centre notifies.

S.5 conditions: (i) monogamy - neither party has a spouse living; (ii) sound mind, capable of valid consent, not suffering from mental disorder unfit for marriage and procreation, no recurrent insanity; (iii) groom 21, bride 18; (iv) not within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits; (v) not sapindas unless custom permits.

Sapinda (S.3(f)): extends to the third generation (inclusive) up the mother's line and the fifth (inclusive) up the father's line. Custom must be ancient, certain, reasonable and not opposed to public policy (S.3(a)).
VOID (S.11): breach of S.5(i), (iv) or (v). Either party may seek a decree of nullity; the marriage is void ab initio even without a decree.

VOIDABLE (S.12): (a) non-consummation due to impotence of the respondent; (b) breach of S.5(ii) (unsound mind etc.); (c) consent obtained by force or fraud (as to nature of ceremony or material fact); (d) respondent pregnant by another person at the time of marriage, petitioner being ignorant. Time limits (S.12(2)): fraud/force petition within one year of discovery/cessation of force and no marital intercourse afterwards; ground (d) within one year of marriage.

Breach of S.5(iii) (age): marriage is neither void nor voidable under HMA; it is punishable (S.18: simple imprisonment up to 15 days or fine up to Rs 1,000). Separately, the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 makes a child marriage voidable at the option of the party who was a child.

Bigamy: S.17 HMA read with BNS S.82 (IPC 494/495). Second marriage is void and punishable (up to 7 years; 10 years if the earlier marriage is concealed). Essential ceremonies of the second marriage must be proved (Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v State of Maharashtra, 1965).

Ceremonies (S.7): marriage is solemnised per customary rites of either party; where saptapadi is part of the rite, the marriage is complete and binding on the seventh step (Priya Bala Ghosh v Suresh Chandra Ghosh, 1971). A registration certificate cannot substitute valid ceremonies (Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal, 2024).
Registration (S.8): for proof only; failure does not invalidate the marriage. Seema v Ashwani Kumar (2006): registration of marriages of all religions was made compulsory by SC directions.

S.16 children: children of void marriages (S.11) and annulled voidable marriages (S.12) are legitimate. They have rights only in the property of their parents (S.16(3)), not of other relatives. Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun (2011; larger-bench reference decided 2023): such children share in the parents' self-acquired property and in the parent's share of coparcenary property on partition.

Jurisdiction (S.19): court where marriage was solemnised, respondent resides, parties last resided together, or (since 2003) where the wife petitioner resides. Transfer under S.21A-21B; day-to-day trial under S.21B.
Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018): S.497 IPC (adultery) struck down; adultery stays a civil wrong and a divorce ground. BNS 2023 does not retain the offence.

provisions.note: Legitimacy of children of void/voidable marriages.

case_laws.name: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v State of Maharashtra
case_laws.holding: Second marriage must be performed with the essential ceremonies for bigamy; invocation of saptapadi where it is part of the rites.

case_laws.name: Priya Bala Ghosh v Suresh Chandra Ghosh
case_laws.holding: Saptapadi is essential only where the customary rites include it.

case_laws.name: Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal
case_laws.holding: A Hindu marriage needs valid ceremonies; a certificate of registration does not validate a marriage without them; marriage is a sacrament, not a commercial event.

case_laws.name: Sarla Mudgal v Union of India
case_laws.holding: A Hindu husband who converts to Islam to marry again is still guilty of bigamy; the first marriage subsists until dissolved under HMA.

case_laws.name: Lily Thomas v Union of India
case_laws.holding: Reaffirmed Sarla Mudgal; conversion does not end a subsisting Hindu marriage.

case_laws.name: Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun
case_laws.holding: Children of void or voidable marriages can claim a share in their parents' property.

case_laws.name: Joseph Shine v Union of India
case_laws.holding: Adultery (S.497 IPC) struck down as violating Arts 14, 15, 21.

traps: Age breach does not make an HMA marriage void; PCMA makes it voidable at the child's option.
S.11 void marriages: only breaches of S.5(i), (iv), (v). S.5(ii) breach is voidable.
Registration is evidentiary, not a validity condition.
Children of void marriages are legitimate but inherit only from their parents.

Voidable = Impotence, Insanity (S.5(ii)), Intimidation/fraud, Illicit pregnancy.

topics.title: Hindu Marriage Act - Matrimonial Reliefs, Divorce Grounds, Mutual Consent and Irretrievable Breakdown
topics.summary: Restitution, judicial separation and divorce, each with grounds, special grounds for wives, the S.13B procedure and the Supreme Court's use of Art 142 for irretrievable breakdown.
key_points: S.9 restitution of conjugal rights: where a spouse has withdrawn from the society of the other without reasonable excuse, the court may decree restitution; the burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the withdrawing spouse. Constitutional validity upheld in Saroj Rani v Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984), overruling T. Sareetha (AP HC, 1983). A fresh challenge (Ojaswa Pathak, 2019) is pending - verify.
S.10 judicial separation: on any ground in S.13(1) (and wife's grounds in S.13(2)); decree can be rescinded on application.

S.13(1) divorce grounds (either spouse): (i) voluntary sexual intercourse with another person (adultery - a single act suffices); (ia) cruelty; (ib) desertion for a continuous period of at least 2 years immediately before the petition; (ii) conversion to another religion; (iii) incurable unsound mind or mental disorder such that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with respondent; (v) venereal disease in communicable form; (vi) renunciation of the world by entering a religious order; (vii) not heard of as alive for 7 years. Leprosy (clause (iv)) was omitted by the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act 2019.
S.13(1A): either party may seek divorce if there has been no resumption of cohabitation for 1 year after a judicial separation decree, or no restitution for 1 year after a restitution decree.

S.13(2) grounds only for the wife: (i) husband had another wife before the Act and she is alive; (ii) husband guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality; (iii) no cohabitation for 1 year after a maintenance decree/order under S.18 HAMA or S.125 CrPC (S.144 BNSS); (iv) option of puberty: married before 15 and repudiated before 18.
S.14 bar: no divorce petition within 1 year of marriage unless exceptional hardship to petitioner or exceptional depravity of respondent (court may allow).

Cruelty: physical or mental conduct of such a kind that cohabitation is harmful or injurious. N.G. Dastane v S. Dastane (1975): standard of proof is preponderance of probabilities. Samar Ghosh v Jaya Ghosh (2007): non-exhaustive illustrations of mental cruelty (persistent unjustifiable conduct, unilateral refusal of intercourse, long separation, false allegations, humiliation). Shobha Rani v Madhukar Reddi (1988): intention is not necessary. K. Srinivas Rao v D.A. Deepa (2013): false criminal complaints (e.g. S.498A) can amount to mental cruelty.

Desertion: factum of separation + animus deserendi + absence of consent or justifying cause + statutory period (Bipinchandra Shah v Prabhavati, 1957; Lachman Utamchand Kirpalani v Meena, 1964). Constructive desertion: the spouse who forces the other to leave is the deserter.

S.13B mutual consent: petition jointly by both; living separately for 1 year or more; unable to live together; mutually agreed to dissolve. The court may grant the decree after 6 months and not later than 18 months from presentation, if the petition is not withdrawn. Consent must continue until the decree (Sureshta Devi v Om Prakash, 1991; Hitesh Bhatnagar v Deepa Bhatnagar, 2011).
Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur (2017): the 6-month period in S.13B(2) is directory and may be waived where the marriage has broken down irretrievably and no chance of reconciliation exists.

Shilpa Sailesh v Varun Sreenivasan (Constitution Bench, 1 May 2023): the Supreme Court may use Art 142 to dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown, waiving the 6-month period and the need for separate proceedings; it is a discretionary power, not a right, and is exercised with attention to the duration of marriage, litigation, attempts at settlement and equities. Irretrievable breakdown is still not a statutory ground (Naveen Kohli v Neelu Kohli, 2006 urged Parliament; Law Commission 71st and 217th Reports).

S.15: remarriage after divorce is allowed once the time for appeal has expired (S.28) or the appeal has been dismissed. S.23: decree conditions (no collusion, no condonation, no taking advantage of own wrong; duty to attempt reconciliation).

S.24 interim maintenance and litigation expenses; S.25 permanent alimony (lump sum or periodic, either spouse may claim); S.26 custody, maintenance and education of children (welfare paramount); S.27 disposal of joint property. Kiran Jyot Maini v Anish Pramod Patel (2024): alimony is for support, not to punish or equalise wealth - verify.

Rajnesh v Neha (2021): guidelines on maintenance - disclosure affidavit of assets and liabilities in all proceedings, maintenance from the date of application, overlapping proceedings, criteria for quantum (status, needs, income, liabilities).

topics.title: Maintenance Across Laws - HAMA, S.144 BNSS (S.125 CrPC), Muslim Women Acts, Senior Citizens Act
topics.summary: Maintenance is a statutory, welfare-oriented right with several parallel routes. Learn who can claim under each, the disqualifications, and the landmark cases (Shah Bano, Danial Latifi, Abdul Samad, Rajnesh v Neha).
key_points: S.144 BNSS (S.125 CrPC; secular): a Magistrate of the first class may order monthly allowance to (a) wife (including a divorced wife who has not remarried), (b) legitimate or illegitimate minor child, (c) adult child unable to maintain self due to physical or mental abnormality or injury, (d) father or mother, where the person with sufficient means neglects or refuses. There is no upper monetary cap (the Rs 500 cap was removed in 2001). Interim maintenance and costs are allowed; allowance runs from the order or, if so ordered, the date of application.

Disqualification of wife (S.144(4) BNSS; S.125(4) CrPC): living in adultery, refusing without sufficient reason to live with husband, or living separately by mutual consent. The wife's own income does not bar the claim unless sufficient (Chaturbhuj v Sita Bai, 2008).

S.144 BNSS is personal-law neutral: Mohd Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985) held that a divorced Muslim wife can claim under it; Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986; Danial Latifi v Union of India (2001) upheld the 1986 Act but read 'reasonable and fair provision' to include future maintenance beyond the iddat; Shabana Bano v Imran Khan (2010) held S.125 CrPC available after iddat; Mohd Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (10 July 2024) held that a divorced Muslim woman can claim under S.125 CrPC (S.144 BNSS) irrespective of the 1986 Act.

HAMA 1956: S.18 - Hindu wife is entitled to maintenance during her lifetime and to live separately without losing it where the husband is guilty of desertion, cruelty, has another wife living, keeps a concubine in the same house or habitually resides with one elsewhere, has converted, or other justifying cause. No claim if she is unchaste or ceases to be a Hindu. S.19: widowed daughter-in-law may claim from the father-in-law if she cannot maintain herself and has no means (obligation is not enforceable if the father-in-law has no ancestral property out of which to maintain). S.20: a Hindu must maintain his legitimate or illegitimate children (until minor) and aged or infirm parents, and unmarried daughters unable to maintain themselves. S.21 dependants; S.22 dependants of deceased; S.23 amount discretionary.

HMA S.24 (interim) and S.25 (permanent alimony) are matrimonial reliefs available to either spouse, even in a void marriage (X v Y, 2025 INSC 197: 'illegitimate wife' and 'faithful mistress' labels are misogynistic; relief under S.25 is discretionary and case specific; interim maintenance is possible when the matrimonial court prima facie finds a marriage void or voidable).

Void marriage and S.125: older view that a woman in a void (bigamous) marriage cannot claim S.125 (Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav, 1988) has been liberalised (Chanmuniya v Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha, 2010 - wife includes a woman in a long-standing live-in relationship; Badshah v Urmila Badshah Godse, 2013).
Rajnesh v Neha (2021): maintenance affidavit of disclosure; same-claim overlap across forums to be disclosed and adjusted; payment enforceable like a decree.
Domestic Violence Act S.20 (monetary relief), S.19 (residence) and S.17 (right to reside in shared household) run alongside and in addition to other remedies (S.26).

Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007: parents (including adoptive and step-parents) and senior citizens (60+) may claim from children or relatives who will inherit; claim before the Maintenance Tribunal (Sub-Divisional Officer), appeal to the Appellate Tribunal (District Magistrate); Tribunal should decide within 90 days; S.9(2) caps the monthly allowance at Rs 10,000 (a 2019 amendment Bill to remove the cap lapsed - verify); S.23: a transfer of property by a senior citizen made on condition of care can be declared void if the transferee fails to maintain (Sudesh Chhikara v Ramti Devi, 2022; Urmila Dixit v Sunil Sharan Dixit, 2025); S.24 abandonment is punishable with up to 3 months and/or fine up to Rs 5,000.

Muslim women's rights on divorce (1986 Act): S.3 mahr, reasonable and fair provision and maintenance during iddat, children's maintenance for 2 years; S.4 maintenance from relatives or State Waqf Board where she cannot maintain herself; S.5 option to be governed by S.125-128 CrPC.

A divorced wife who has remarried loses S.125 rights; one who has not remarried retains them.

topics.title: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956 - Adoption; Adoption under JJ Act 2015
topics.summary: The Act is the most 'section-number' heavy part of Hindu law. Learn who can adopt, who can give, who can be adopted, the other conditions, effects and the secular JJ Act route.
key_points: S.6: valid adoption needs (i) the adopter's capacity and right to adopt, (ii) the giver's capacity to give, (iii) the adoptee's capacity to be adopted, and (iv) compliance with other conditions.

S.7 male: any Hindu male of sound mind who is not a minor may adopt; if married, with the consent of his wife (or all wives), unless she has entirely and finally renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu or been declared of unsound mind. S.8 female: a Hindu female of sound mind and not a minor, if unmarried, or if married, whose marriage has been dissolved, whose husband is dead, has finally renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu or been declared of unsound mind. A married woman cannot adopt in her own right during the subsistence of marriage.

S.9 who may give: father or mother or guardian. The father cannot give without the mother's consent unless she has renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu or is of unsound mind. A guardian can give only with court permission where both parents are dead, have renounced the world, abandoned the child, are of unsound mind or the parentage is unknown. The mother can give if the father is dead or disqualified.
S.10 who may be adopted: a Hindu, not already adopted, not married (unless custom), and not completed the age of 15 (unless custom allows).

S.11 other conditions: for adoption of a son the adopter must not have a Hindu son, son's son or son's son's son (legitimate or adopted) living; for a daughter, no Hindu daughter or son's daughter living; where the adopter is a male and the adoptee a female (or vice versa), the adopter must be at least 21 years older; the same child cannot be adopted by two persons simultaneously; the child must be actually given and taken (datta homam is not essential).

S.12 effects: from the date of adoption the child is deemed the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes and ties with the family of birth are severed; the child cannot marry any person he or she could not marry in the natural family; property vested in the child before adoption continues; the child cannot divest any person of an estate vested before adoption.

S.13 adopters' right to dispose of property is unaffected; S.14 where a male Hindu with more than one wife adopts, the seniormost in marriage is the adoptive mother; S.15 a valid adoption cannot be cancelled by anyone; S.16 presumption of validity of a registered adoption deed; S.17 payments for adoption are prohibited (punishable).

Adoption under the JJ (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015: secular; Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) regulates; Adoption Regulations 2022; the 2021 amendment empowers the District Magistrate to issue adoption orders (instead of courts). Shabnam Hashmi v Union of India (2014): any person may adopt under the JJ Act irrespective of religion; this is an enabling law and does not displace personal laws.

Proof: Sawan Ram v Kalawati (1967) - proof of giving and taking; recitals in a registered deed carry a presumption but are rebuttable. Lakshmi Kant Pandey v Union of India (1984) - guidelines on inter-country adoption.

topics.title: Guardianship and Custody - Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956; Guardians and Wards Act 1890
topics.summary: Natural guardians, limits on a guardian's powers over immovable property, and the supremacy of the welfare principle in custody disputes.
key_points: S.4 HMGA: minor = person who has not completed 18 years. The Act supplements (does not replace) the Guardians and Wards Act 1890.

S.6 natural guardians: for a boy or unmarried girl - the father, and after him the mother; but custody of a minor who has not completed 5 years shall ordinarily be with the mother. For an illegitimate boy or unmarried girl - the mother, and after her the father. For a married girl - the husband. No guardian can be appointed for the minor's undivided interest in joint family property managed by an adult member (S.12).

Gita Hariharan v Reserve Bank of India (1999): 'after' in S.6(a) means 'in the absence of', i.e. the father's absence or disinterest, not after his death; the mother can act as natural guardian even during the father's lifetime if the father is indifferent or incapable. Jijabai Vithalrao Gajre v Pathankhan (1970) took a similar view. ABC v State (NCT of Delhi) (2015): an unwed mother can be the sole guardian and need not name the father.
S.7: adoptive father, and after him adoptive mother, is natural guardian of an adopted son. S.9: testamentary guardian appointed by will (father, or mother where the father is dead/unfit).

S.8 powers of natural guardian: may do all acts necessary or reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or the minor's estate, but cannot bind the minor by a personal covenant. Without the previous permission of the court, the guardian cannot (a) mortgage, charge, sell, gift, exchange or transfer immovable property of the minor, or (b) lease it for over 5 years or beyond 1 year after the minor attains majority. A transfer in breach is voidable at the instance of the minor or any person claiming under him (S.8(3)). Court permission only for necessity or evident advantage (S.8(4)).

S.11: a de facto guardian (a person who is not a lawful guardian) cannot deal with the minor's property. S.13: welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration; no right under the Act or any law supersedes it.

Guardians and Wards Act 1890: S.7 (appointment/declaration), S.8 (who may apply), S.17 (court considers the minor's welfare, age, sex, religion, character, preference of an intelligent minor), S.19 (no appointment if the father is fit and alive), S.25 (return of ward who leaves or is removed from the guardian's custody), S.26 (removal of ward from jurisdiction), S.4(1) (minor under 18).

Custody principles: Gaurav Nagpal v Sumedha Nagpal (2009), Nil Ratan Kundu v Abhijit Kundu (2008) - welfare, not parental rights, decides; Roxann Sharma v Arun Sharma (2015) - child under 5 with mother; Vikram Vir Vohra v Shalini Bhalla (2010) - shared parenting; Yashita Sahu v State of Rajasthan (2020) - visitation and custody; Tejaswini Gaud v Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari (2019) - habeas corpus for child custody is a summary remedy and welfare decides; Prateek Gupta v Shilpi Gupta (2017) and V. Ravi Chandran v Union of India (2010) - foreign custody orders are not binding and the child's welfare is examined by the Indian court.

Family Courts Act 1984: family courts decide guardianship and custody matters (S.7); proceedings are confidential and conciliatory (S.9, 10); no right to legal representation as of right (S.13); appeal lies to the High Court within 30 days (S.19).

topics.title: Hindu Succession Act 1956 (as amended 2005) and the Joint Family
topics.summary: Intestate succession of Hindu males and females, daughters' coparcenary rights (S.6), woman's absolute ownership (S.14), and the character of property inherited under S.8.
key_points: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 (in force 9 September 2005): S.6 makes a daughter a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with the same rights and liabilities; S.23 (restriction on daughter's right to a dwelling house) and S.24 (widow's remarriage disqualification) omitted; S.4(2) (agricultural land exemption) omitted.

Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020, three judges): the daughter's coparcenary right is by birth; it is not necessary that the father was alive on 9 September 2005; Prakash v Phulavati (2016) overruled to that extent; Danamma @ Suman Surpur v Amar (2018) partly overruled. A partition claimed by oral evidence is not accepted unless supported by public documents or a court decree (partition is a registered deed or a decree; S.6(5) Explanation). Daughters have equal rights in Mitakshara coparcenary property and can claim partition.

Arunachala Gounder v Ponnusamy (2022): self-acquired property of a Hindu male dying intestate (including before 1956) devolves by inheritance; a daughter inherits it, and on her death without issue it goes to her father's heirs (S.15(2)(b)).

S.8 (intestate male): property devolves first on Class I heirs, then Class II, then agnates, then cognates. Class I (16 heirs after 2005): son, daughter, widow, mother, son and daughter of a predeceased son, son and daughter of a predeceased daughter, widow of a predeceased son, widow of a predeceased son of a predeceased son and the four added in 2005 (children of predeceased daughter of predeceased daughter and children of predeceased son of predeceased daughter, etc.). Father is not Class I - he is the first entry in Class II (so mother inherits, father does not, unless no Class I heir exists).

S.10 distribution among Class I: the widow(s) together take one share, each son one, each daughter one, each branch of a predeceased son/daughter one share jointly, mother one share. S.9: Class I heirs take simultaneously and exclude all others.

S.14 woman's property: any property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act, is held by her as full owner and not as a limited owner. S.14(2) exception: property acquired by gift, will, instrument, decree or award where the instrument expressly prescribes a restricted estate. V. Tulasamma v Sesha Reddy (1977): property given to a widow in lieu of maintenance becomes absolute under S.14(1).

S.15 (intestate female): first sons, daughters (and children of predeceased children) and the husband; then heirs of the husband; then mother and father; then heirs of the father; then heirs of the mother. S.15(2): property inherited from her father or mother, in absence of children, goes to the father's heirs; property inherited from her husband or father-in-law, in absence of children, goes to the husband's heirs.

Disqualifications: S.25 murderer; S.26 descendants of a convert (the convert himself is not disqualified); S.27 other disqualifications; disease, defect and unchastity are not grounds (S.28). S.30 allows testamentary disposition of coparcenary interest.

Joint family and coparcenary: HUF = all lineal descendants of a common ancestor, wives and unmarried daughters; coparcenary = the narrower body of the propositus and three generations of male lineal descendants (now daughters included by birth). Mitakshara - rights by birth and survivorship (modified); Dayabhaga - rights by death, no right by birth. Karta: the manager; alienation of coparcenary property only for legal necessity, benefit of the estate or indispensable duties (Hanooman Prasad Pandey v Babooee Munraj Koonwari, 1856 PC); gifts only of a small portion for pious purposes (Kamla Devi v Bachulal Gupta, 1957). A woman can be karta (Sujata Sharma v Manu Gupta, Delhi HC, 2015).

Darubai v Kamalabai (2026 INSC 613, reported 3 June 2026; Karol and Masih JJ): property inherited under S.8 does not acquire coparcenary character; the heirs take as tenants in common with defined shares; karta-ship does not arise from mere descent from a paternal ancestor; one heir cannot sell the shares of the others as karta. It follows Yudhishter v Ashok Kumar (1987) and Uttam v Saubhag Singh (2016). The Court also (2026) reportedly held that the 2005 amendment does not limit daughters' pre-existing inheritance rights - verify.

S.6(4) after 2005: no pious obligation of a son or grandson to pay a father's or grandfather's debts, but debts contracted before 2005 are protected. S.6(3): on a coparcener's death after 2005 the interest devolves by testamentary or intestate succession, not survivorship.

topics.title: Muslim Law I - Sources, Marriage (Nikah), Mahr, Maintenance
topics.summary: Sources and schools; validity of nikah; mahr as an obligation of the husband; and the wife's rights during marriage.
key_points: Sources: Quran, Sunnah/Hadith, Ijma (consensus), Qiyas (analogical deduction); secondary: Urf (custom), Istihsan, Istislah. Sunni schools: Hanafi (most Indian Muslims), Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali; Shias: Ithna Ashari (Twelvers), Ismaili, Zaidi.

Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937: S.2 applies Muslim law (in cases where parties are Muslims) to intestate succession, special property of females, marriage, dissolution of marriage (talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula, mubarat), maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts and waqfs; customary law is excluded in these matters. It does not cover wills and adoption unless the person makes a declaration under S.3 (as originally framed).

Nikah is a civil contract: proposal (ijab) and acceptance (qubul) at the same meeting, free consent, competence (puberty, sound mind), witnesses (Sunni: two male or one male and two females; Shia: none required). No religious ceremony or writing is essential.

Classification of marriages: valid (sahih), irregular (fasid), void (batil). Irregular: absence of witnesses, marriage during iddat of another, with a woman of a non-Kitabiya religion (for male), fifth wife, unlawful conjunction. An irregular marriage can be regularised by removing the impediment; if consummated it carries limited effects (proper dower or specified dower whichever is less, legitimate children, iddat). Void: marriage within prohibited degrees (consanguinity, affinity, fosterage) - no legal consequences. Muta (temporary) marriage is recognised only by Shias (Ithna Ashari).

Capacity and age: puberty (presumed at 15 years) under classical law; guardianship in marriage (wilayat) of a minor by father or paternal relatives; the minor's option of puberty (khyar-ul-bulugh). The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 applies to all communities in principle; Society for Enlightenment and Voluntary Action v Union of India (Oct 2024) issued guidelines for enforcing the PCMA - the Court did not resolve the personal-law conflict (verify).

Mahr (dower): an obligation imposed by law on the husband as a mark of respect to the wife (Abdul Kadir v Salima, 1886); not a consideration for marriage; marriage is valid even if mahr is not fixed (proper/customary dower payable). Types: specified, proper (mahr-i-misl), prompt (muajjal), deferred (muwajjal). Hanafi minimum: 10 dirhams (Maliki 3); no maximum. Wife may refuse cohabitation until prompt dower is paid. On dissolution, unpaid dower is a debt.

Widow's right of retention (lien): if the widow is in lawful possession of the husband's property, she may retain it until her dower is paid; the lien is not a right of ownership and cannot be transferred (Hamira Bibi v Zubaida Bibi, 1916).

Maintenance (nafaqah): husband must maintain his wife during marriage (even if she is wealthy) unless she is disobedient (nashiza); also minor children and indigent parents; wife not entitled if she refuses to cohabit without lawful reason. Statutory remedies: S.144 BNSS (S.125 CrPC), Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986.

Guardianship and custody: father is natural guardian of the person and property; mother has the right of hizanat (physical custody) - Hanafi: boy till 7, girl until puberty; Shia: boy till 2, girl till 7; custody can be lost on remarriage to a stranger or on bad character; welfare of the child prevails in practice.

topics.title: Muslim Law II - Divorce: Talaq, Khula, Mubarat, DMMA 1939, 2019 Act
topics.summary: Forms of divorce, the Supreme Court's decision on instant triple talaq (Shayara Bano), the 2019 Act, judicial divorce under DMMA 1939, and the pending talaq-e-hasan challenge.
key_points: Talaq by husband: talaq-ul-sunnat - (a) ahsan: a single pronouncement in a tuhr (period of purity), followed by abstention from intercourse during the iddat; revocable until iddat ends; (b) hasan: three successive pronouncements in three successive tuhrs, the divorce becoming irrevocable on the third. Talaq-ul-biddat (triple talaq/instant talaq): three pronouncements in one tuhr or a single irrevocable pronouncement.

Shayara Bano v Union of India (22 Aug 2017, 3:2): instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) is void and unconstitutional (Kurian Joseph, Nariman and Lalit JJ held it arbitrary/not part of essential Islamic practice or violative of Art 14; Khehar CJ and Nazeer J dissented). Earlier cases: Rukia Khatoon v Abdul Khalique Laskar (1981) - talaq must be for a reason and preceded by reconciliation attempts; Shamim Ara v State of U.P. (2002) - same, and talaq must be proved.

Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019: S.3 instant triple talaq (spoken, written, electronic) is void and illegal; S.4 punishment up to 3 years' imprisonment and fine; offence is cognizable only on information by the married woman or her blood/marriage relatives; the Magistrate may grant bail only after hearing the woman; compoundable at the woman's instance with the Magistrate's permission; she is entitled to subsistence allowance and custody of minor children.

Talaq-e-hasan: the husband pronounces talaq once a month over three months. Challenged before the Supreme Court (Benazeer Heena v Union of India and connected pleas); in 2026 the Court referred a related dispute to mediation (Justice Kurian Joseph) and on 16 October 2026 a bench of the CJI and Justice Bagchi sought the Centre's response on a plea for uniform procedural safeguards for all forms of talaq and clubbed it with the pending petition (verify the current status).

Delegated talaq (talaq-i-tafweez): the husband delegates the power to the wife (or a third party) to divorce herself on specified conditions. Ila (vow of abstinence for 4 months), zihar (comparing wife to a prohibited relative; wife may seek judicial decree if the husband does not atone) and lian (false accusation of adultery; divorce by court decree) are other forms; DMMA S.2(ix) covers them.

Khula: divorce at the instance of the wife with the husband's consent in return for consideration (often release of mahr); mubarat: mutual desire of both; both are irrevocable divorces (talaq-i-bain) with iddat after. The wife's right to khula without husband's consent is recognised by Kerala High Court (K.C. Moyin v Nafeesa, 1972; Full Bench 2021) - verify.

Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 S.2 grounds (decree for wife): (i) whereabouts of husband unknown for 4 years; (ii) failure to maintain for 2 years; (iii) husband's imprisonment for 7 years or more (after sentence final); (iv) failure to perform marital obligations for 3 years without reasonable cause; (v) impotency at marriage and continuing; (vi) insanity for 2 years or virulent venereal disease (leprosy omitted 2019); (vii) option of puberty - married before 15, repudiated before 18, not consummated; (viii) cruelty (habitual assault, associating with women of ill repute, forcing immoral life, disposing of her property, obstructing religious practice, unequal treatment of co-wives); (ix) any other ground valid under Muslim law (includes lian, ila, zihar, talaq-i-tafweez).

DMMA S.4: apostasy by a Muslim wife does not itself dissolve marriage; S.5: wife's dower rights are not affected. Conversion of a non-Muslim wife (other than Kitabiya) to Islam and reversion: see S.4 proviso.

Iddat: divorced woman - 3 menstrual courses (or 3 lunar months if not subject to menstruation); widow - 4 months 10 days; pregnant - until delivery. Remarriage prohibited during iddat; a marriage during iddat is irregular (fasid). Halala: a fixed-term marital practice to remarry a thrice-divorced wife; the Uttarakhand UCC 2024 bans it - verify.

Polygamy: up to four wives under personal law (Quranic condition: equal treatment); the Supreme Court has repeatedly urged a UCC (Jorden Diengdeh v S.S. Chopra, 1985; Sarla Mudgal, 1995). State UCCs (Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Assam) prohibit polygamy for their residents (non-tribal) - see 6A-13.

topics.title: Muslim Law III - Gifts (Hiba), Wills (Wasiyat), Waqf, Pre-emption, Inheritance
topics.summary: Property law of Muslims: hiba needs delivery of possession; wills are limited to one-third; waqf is a pious endowment now governed by the Waqf Act 1995 as amended in 2025; pre-emption has three demands; inheritance has no representation.
key_points: Hiba (gift): requisites - (i) declaration by donor, (ii) acceptance by donee (express or implied), (iii) delivery of possession (actual or constructive). Writing and registration are not required for a Muslim gift (S.129 TPA preserves the rule); a registered deed without delivery is not enough. Gift of future property is void; gift of undivided share (musha) in a divisible property is irregular under Hanafi law but valid in indivisible property. Gift by a donor to his minor child may be completed by declaration if the donor is the guardian (Hafeeza Bibi v Shaikh Mohammad Farooq, 2011 - possession/declaration). Gift is revocable by the donor (except in cases such as gift to a relative within prohibited degrees, gift by husband to wife, gift for consideration). Hiba-bil-iwaz (gift for consideration) is a sale in effect; hiba-ba-shart-ul-iwaz is a gift with a condition of return; sadaqah is a gift for pious purposes.

Marz-ul-maut (death-illness): a gift made while apprehending death from the illness that actually causes death is governed by the rules of wills - limited to one-third of the net estate, and a gift to an heir needs the consent of the other heirs; delivery required.

Wills (wasiyat): Sunni - a bequest is valid only up to one-third of the net estate (after funeral expenses and debts) without the consent of heirs; a bequest to an heir needs the consent of the other heirs (given after the testator's death); a will may be oral; consent of heirs not needed for bequest to a stranger up to 1/3. Shia - bequest to an heir up to 1/3 is valid without the consent of other heirs; a bequest in excess of 1/3 needs ratification. The bequest to a person not in existence is void unless the person is born within six months. A bequest in favour of a murderer-legatee is invalid (Sunni).

Waqf: permanent dedication of property by a person professing Islam for a purpose recognised as religious, pious or charitable (S.3(r) Waqf Act 1995). Modes: declaration (oral or written), usage (waqf by user - prospectively removed by the 2025 amendment), endowment by will (within 1/3), mortgage/ immemorial usage. Waqf-alal-aulad (family waqf) is valid under the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act 1913, provided the ultimate benefit is for the poor. The mutawalli is a manager, not an owner (can be removed for breach). Waqf Board and Tribunal supervise. Property once waqf is inalienable.

Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 (renames the 1995 Act as the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act): in an interim order of 15 September 2025 (2025 INSC 1116, CJI Gavai and Masih J), the Supreme Court did not stay the Act as a whole but stayed: the requirement that a waqf donor must have practised Islam for 5 years (until rules prescribe a determination process); the proviso to S.3C(2) (property under inquiry not treated as waqf) and S.3C(3)-(4) (officer to correct revenue records), pending a Waqf Tribunal decision. It capped non-Muslim members at 4 of 22 in the Central Waqf Council and 3 of 11 in a State Waqf Board. It did not stay the removal of 'waqf by user' (prospective), S.3D (protected monuments), S.3E (Scheduled Tribes land), mandatory deed and registration, and the application of the Limitation Act. Final decision: pending in the sources reviewed - verify.

Pre-emption (shufa): the right of a co-owner or neighbour to purchase property sold to a stranger by substituting himself for the buyer. Classes: shafi-i-sharik (co-sharer), shafi-i-khalit (participator in appendages/immunities such as a right of way), shafi-i-jar (adjoining neighbour). Three demands: talab-i-mowasibat (immediate demand), talab-i-ishhad (demand with witnesses), talab-i-khusumat (filing suit). Pre-emption is a weak right, defeated by any legitimate means (Bishan Singh v Khazan Singh, 1958); Bhau Ram v Baij Nath Singh (1962) upheld pre-emption on ground of vicinage as a reasonable restriction (then Art 19(1)(f)). Hindu and Christian law do not recognise pre-emption by custom except where custom exists.

Inheritance (Sunni/Hanafi): three classes - Sharers (Quranic heirs; 12: husband, wife, daughter, son's daughter, father, mother, true grandfather, true grandmother, full sister, consanguine sister, uterine brother, uterine sister), Residuaries (agnatic, e.g. son, father, brother), Distant kindred (dhawul arham). There is no representation (a grandchild is excluded if a son of the deceased is alive) and no distinction of birth rights. Wife: 1/8 with children, 1/4 without; husband: 1/4 with children, 1/2 without; mother: 1/6 with children or two or more siblings, otherwise 1/3; father: 1/6 with son; daughter alone 1/2, two or more 2/3 jointly; a daughter with a son becomes residuary and takes half of the son's share. Doctrines: awl (proportionate reduction when shares exceed unity) and radd (return of surplus to sharers). Shias do not follow the Asaba (residuary) system; they distribute among three classes of heirs by nearness of relationship. A murderer is disqualified (Sunni); apostasy and conversion no longer disqualify (Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850).
Women's property: Muslim women own and dispose of property absolutely and independently of the husband; a wife's mahr is a debt.

topics.title: Christian and Parsi Law - Marriage, Divorce, Succession
topics.summary: Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872, Indian Divorce Act 1869, Indian Succession Act 1925 (Christians and Parsis) and the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936.
key_points: Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872: applies where at least one party is a Christian; marriage is solemnised by a minister of the church, a clergyman, a Marriage Registrar or a licensed person; marriage age: groom 21 and bride 18; notice and publication requirements; marriage registered. A marriage solemnised in breach is void in certain cases.

Indian Divorce Act 1869 (applies where the petitioner or respondent professes Christianity): S.10 divorce grounds (adultery, cruelty, desertion for 2 years, unsound mind, venereal disease, conversion/failure to comply with restitution decree, wife's grounds including rape, sodomy, bestiality). The 2001 Amendment (Indian Divorce (Amendment) Act 2001) equalised grounds for husband and wife (earlier, the wife needed adultery plus another ground - struck down in Ammini E.J. v Union of India, Kerala HC 1995); it inserted S.10A: divorce by mutual consent after separation for 2 years or more (compare 1 year under HMA and SMA). Leprosy was omitted from the 1869 Act by the 2019 Act - verify.
Alimony under the Divorce Act: S.36 interim alimony and S.37 permanent alimony (up to 1/5th of husband's average income); custody S.41.

Christian intestate succession (ISA 1925, Part V, Chapter II): widow takes 1/3 of the estate and lineal descendants take the remaining 2/3 (S.33(a)); if there are no lineal descendants but there are kindred, widow takes 1/2 and kindred 1/2 (S.33(b)); if there are no descendants or kindred, the widow takes the entire estate (S.33(c)); children take equally; no preference of sons over daughters. Mary Roy v State of Kerala (1986): Travancore Christian Succession Act 1916 was superseded by the ISA 1925; daughters now share equally with sons.

Wills (ISA 1925, Part VI): S.59 competent testator (sound mind, not minor); S.63 execution - signed by testator (or by another in his presence and by his direction) with a mark if illiterate, and attested by two or more witnesses, each of whom has seen the testator sign; wills of a Christian or any non-Hindu are governed by ISA irrespective of religion. S.118 (bequest to religious or charitable uses within a certain time before death) was struck down in John Vallamattom v Union of India (2003) as violating Art 14 and 25.

Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936: S.3 conditions - monogamy, no prohibited relationship, age 21 for male and 18 for female, solemnised by a priest (Dastur) in the presence of two Parsi witnesses (Ashirvad ceremony); S.4 bigamy void and punishable (S.5); a Parsi who ceases to be a Parsi by conversion may be sued for divorce (S.32(j)).

Parsi divorce (S.32): (a) non-consummation within 1 year due to wilful refusal; (b) unsound mind at the time of marriage and continuing; (c) wife pregnant by another at marriage; (d) adultery, fornication, bigamy, rape or unnatural offence by respondent; (dd) cruelty; (e) hurt/venereal disease; (f) husband guilty of rape; (g) imprisonment of 7 years or more; (h) desertion for 2 years; (i) failure to comply with a decree for separate maintenance for 1 year; (j) conversion; S.32B mutual consent after 1 year of marriage. Matrimonial courts consist of a judge with Parsi delegates.

Parsi intestate succession (ISA 1925 S.50-56): widow and children take equal shares (a widow takes a share equal to each child); parents take a half share of a child's share; no distinction between sons and daughters; rules differ if the intestate is a Parsi woman (husband or widower takes a child-equal share).
Jews and others: Indian Succession Act governs; Jewish law is uncodified and applied as custom.

topics.title: Special Marriage Act 1954
topics.summary: Secular civil marriage for any two persons (including inter-faith couples) with a notice procedure, plus registration of existing marriages and divorce provisions.
key_points: S.4 conditions: (a) neither party has a spouse living; (b) neither is incapable of giving valid consent due to unsoundness of mind, nor suffering from mental disorder making them unfit for marriage and procreation, nor subject to recurrent insanity; (c) groom 21 and bride 18; (d) parties not within prohibited degrees (unless custom permits one party's religion);

Procedure: notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where one party has resided for at least 30 days (S.5); the notice is published for 30 days (S.6-7); objections within 30 days (S.7); inquiry (S.8); marriage solemnised within 3 months of the notice (S.14 - fresh notice if lapsed); solemnisation in the presence of three witnesses and the Marriage Officer (S.11-13); certificate is conclusive evidence (S.13). The Allahabad High Court in Safiya Sultana v State of U.P. (2021) held that publication of notice is optional at the request of the parties; the Supreme Court has recognised the right to marry a person of one's choice as part of Art 21 (Lata Singh v State of U.P., 2006; Shafin Jahan v Asokan K.M., 2018).

S.15-18: registration of marriages solemnised in other forms - conditions: a ceremony was performed; neither party has a spouse; neither is of unsound mind; both completed age; not within prohibited degrees; parties have resided in the district for 30 days; registration makes the marriage a marriage under the Act.

S.19: marriage solemnised under the Act of a member of an undivided family professing Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain religion is deemed to effect his severance from the family. S.21: succession to property of persons married under the Act and their issue is governed by the Indian Succession Act 1925; S.21A: where both are Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain, the Hindu Succession Act applies instead.

Matrimonial reliefs: S.22 restitution; S.23 judicial separation; S.24 void marriages (breach of S.4(a), (b), (c), (d)... void conditions); S.25 voidable marriages (non-consummation due to wilful refusal; respondent pregnant by another; consent by force or fraud; mental disorder); S.27 divorce grounds (adultery, desertion for 2 years, imprisonment for 7 years, cruelty, unsound mind, venereal disease; wife's grounds - rape, sodomy, bestiality, non-compliance with a maintenance decree); S.28 mutual consent after 1 year of separation, with the 6-18 month process as under HMA (Amardeep Singh principles apply); S.36 interim alimony and S.37 permanent alimony.

Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v Union of India (17 October 2023, Constitution Bench): no fundamental right to marry; the Court declined to read down or strike down provisions of the SMA to include same-sex marriage; it left the question to Parliament; the Union assured a committee on rights of queer couples; review petitions were dismissed in January 2025 (verify). The Court recognised that queer couples have the right to cohabit and non-discrimination; CARA regulation barring single/queer adoptions stays.

Interfaith couples: the SMA does not require conversion; several states' anti-conversion laws require declarations for conversions, not for SMA marriages; Shakti Vahini v Union of India (2018) and Lata Singh protect adult choice and direct protective measures against honour crimes.

topics.title: Domestic Violence Act 2005, Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, Cruelty and Dowry Death (BNS), Child Marriage Act 2006
topics.summary: Protective statutes for women in the family: definitions, reliefs, penalties and the leading cases.
key_points: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (in force 26 October 2006): civil remedy with a criminal enforcement component. 'Aggrieved person' (S.2(a)) is a woman who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent (marriage, relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, joint family) and alleges domestic violence. Respondent (S.2(q)): any adult male; the words 'adult male' were struck down in Hiral P. Harsora v Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016) - women can be respondents. Domestic violence (S.3) includes physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse and harassment for dowry. Shared household (S.2(s)): where the woman lives or has lived in a domestic relationship, whether or not she has title - Satish Chander Ahuja v Sneha Ahuja (2020) overruled S.R. Batra v Taruna Batra (2007) on narrow reading.

Reliefs: protection orders (S.18), residence orders (S.19), monetary relief (S.20), custody orders (S.21), compensation (S.22), interim and ex parte orders (S.23). Application to the Magistrate (S.12); the court shall fix first hearing within 3 days and endeavour to dispose within 60 days (S.12(5)); Protection Officer (S.8-9), service providers (S.10), counselling and in-camera proceedings; breach of a protection order is an offence (S.31) - imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 20,000 or both; appeal to Sessions Court in 30 days (S.29). Remedies under the Act are in addition to other laws (S.26). D. Velusamy v D. Patchaiammal (2010) and Indra Sarma v V.K.V. Sarma (2013): 'relationship in the nature of marriage' needs holding out as spouses, legal age to marry, being qualified to marry, voluntary cohabitation for a significant period; a casual or 'keep' relationship is outside the Act.

Dowry Prohibition Act 1961: 'dowry' means property given or agreed to be given directly or indirectly at, before or after marriage in connection with the marriage (S.2); gifts given without demand are outside the definition, subject to list-keeping rules. S.3: giving, taking or abetting dowry - at least 5 years' imprisonment and fine of not less than Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more; S.4: demanding dowry - 6 months to 2 years and fine up to Rs 10,000; S.4A banned advertisements; S.6 dowry to be transferred to the woman within 3 months, held in trust; S.8: offences are cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable; S.8A burden of proof on the person who takes or demands dowry; S.8B Dowry Prohibition Officers.

Cruelty by husband or relatives: S.85 BNS (S.498A IPC) - up to 3 years and fine; S.86 BNS defines cruelty (wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury, or harassment to coerce her or her relatives to meet unlawful demands for property or valuable security). Dowry death: S.80 BNS (S.304B IPC) - death of a woman within 7 years of marriage by burns or bodily injury or otherwise than under normal circumstances, with cruelty or harassment soon before death in connection with dowry; punishment 7 years to life; presumption under S.118 BSA (S.113B IEA). Abetment of suicide: S.108 BNS (S.306 IPC); S.117 BSA presumption within 7 years of marriage. S.82 BNS - bigamy.

Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014): police must not arrest automatically for offences punishable up to 7 years; apply S.41 CrPC (S.35 BNSS) and record reasons. Preeti Gupta v State of Jharkhand (2010) and Dara Lakshmi Narayana v State of Telangana (2024): warn against misuse by exaggerated or omnibus allegations; Rajesh Sharma v State of U.P. (2017) (Family Welfare Committees) was modified by Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v Union of India (2018). Rupali Devi v State of U.P. (2019): the court at the wife's refuge place has territorial jurisdiction over mental cruelty offences. Satvir Singh v State of Punjab (2001) and Kans Raj v State of Punjab (2000): 'soon before death' means a proximate and live link, no fixed period.

Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006: child = male under 21, female under 18. Child marriage is voidable at the option of the child party, by petition to the district court within 2 years after attaining majority (S.3); void in certain cases (S.12: child taken away from guardian by enticement or force, sold for marriage, or trafficked for immoral purposes). S.4: maintenance and residence to the female contracting party until remarriage; S.5-6: custody, maintenance and legitimacy of children. Punishments: S.9 adult male above 18 marrying a child, S.10 solemnising, S.11 promoting or permitting - rigorous imprisonment up to 2 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh (no imprisonment for a woman for S.9-10). S.13 injunction power; S.15 offences cognizable and non-bailable; Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (S.16). Independent Thought v Union of India (2017): sexual intercourse with a wife aged 15-18 is rape (Exception 2 read down); BNS S.63 exception 2 now sets the age at 18. Marital rape of an adult wife is still excepted (challenge pending in the Supreme Court - verify).

Other: Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021 (altruistic surrogacy only, intending married couple, five years of marriage and infertility certificate; woman 25-50 and man 26-55 years) and the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act 2021 - peripheral; the Supreme Court in 2025 relaxed the age limits for couples who had begun the process before the Act (verify).

topics.summary: Art 44, judicial calls for a UCC, and the state UCC laws (Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Assam) are active current-affairs hooks.
key_points: Art 44 (DPSP): the State shall endeavour to secure a UCC for citizens throughout India. Art 25-26 protect religious freedom; personal laws and Part III: State of Bombay v Narasu Appa Mali (1952) held personal laws are not 'laws in force' under Art 13; contrary views in later cases. Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act 2024: passed February 2024 and operationalised 27 January 2025 - first state UCC. Covers marriage age 21/18, mandatory registration of marriages and live-in relationships, ban on polygamy and halala, equal intestate succession (Class I heirs), and rights of children of live-in relationships; excludes Scheduled Tribes. mcqs.explain: S.7 proviso.

A gift to the wife's father

mcqs.explain: S.3(3) - before the petitioner completes two years after attaining majority.

options: Same-sex marriage is valid under the SMA

mcqs.explain: Constitution Bench, 17 October 2023; matter left to Parliament.

mcqs.explain: A divorced wife who has not remarried is a 'wife' for maintenance.

sections.title: Cyber Law

background.summary: Cyber Law for AIBE is essentially the Information Technology Act 2000 (as amended in 2008) plus its Rules, supplemented by constitutional privacy law (Puttaswamy), the DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025, and the cyber-relevant provisions of the BNS, BNSS and BSA. With only 2 questions, the dependable marks are S.66A/Shreya Singhal, the offence-and-punishment table (S.65-67B, 66C-66F), S.79 safe harbour, the First Schedule exclusions, definitions and digital signatures; the current-affairs mark is the DPDP Act/Rules or the IT Rules amendments.
background.approach: Memorise the offence table in 6B-2 first (it covers most past questions), then S.79 and Shreya Singhal, then the DPDP penalty/child/Board facts, then definitions and authorities.

topics.title: Information Technology Act 2000 - Scope, Definitions, Electronic Records, Digital and Electronic Signatures, E-Governance
topics.summary: The IT Act gives legal recognition to electronic transactions (based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce, 1996), creates the digital signature regime and the cyber-offence framework. Amended substantially in 2008 (in force 27 October 2009).
key_points: Enacted 2000 (in force 17 October 2000). Objects: legal recognition for e-commerce and e-records, facilitate e-governance, amend the IPC, Evidence Act, Bankers' Books Evidence Act and RBI Act. Extends to the whole of India and, under S.1(2) read with S.75, applies to an offence or contravention committed outside India by any person if the act involves a computer, computer system or network located in India.

Exclusions (S.1(4), First Schedule): (1) negotiable instrument (other than a cheque), (2) power of attorney, (3) trust, (4) will or testamentary disposition, (5) contract for sale or conveyance of immovable property or any interest in it. An electronic cheque is not excluded.

Key definitions (S.2): 'computer', 'computer network', 'computer resource', 'data', 'communication device' (S.2(1)(ha)), 'cyber security' (S.2(1)(nb)), 'electronic record' (S.2(1)(t)), 'electronic signature' (S.2(1)(ta)), 'digital signature' (S.2(1)(p)), 'originator', 'addressee', 'subscriber' and 'intermediary' (S.2(1)(w): any person who on behalf of another receives, stores or transmits an electronic record or provides a service relating to it - telecom, network, internet and web-hosting service providers, search engines, online payment, auction and marketplace sites and cyber cafes).

Digital signature (S.3): authentication of an electronic record by a subscriber using an asymmetric crypto system and hash function (public/private key pair). Electronic signature (S.3A, 2008): any technology specified in the Second Schedule (e.g. Aadhaar e-KYC e-sign). Digital Signature Certificate: issued by a Certifying Authority (S.35).

Chapter III e-governance: S.4 legal recognition of electronic records; S.5 of electronic signatures; S.6 use in government and its agencies; S.6A delivery of services by service providers (Common Service Centres); S.7 retention of electronic records; S.7A audit; S.8 publication in the Gazette in electronic form; S.10A (2008): contracts formed through electronic means are not unenforceable merely because electronic form was used.

Chapter IV attribution, acknowledgement and dispatch: S.11 attribution (an electronic record is that of the originator if sent by him, by an authorised person or by an automated system); S.12 acknowledgement of receipt; S.13 time and place of dispatch (when it enters a computer resource outside the originator's control) and receipt (when it enters the designated computer resource); place is the place of business of the originator/addressee.

Chapters V-VI secure electronic records and signatures (S.14-16) and Regulation of Certifying Authorities (S.17-34): Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) appointed under S.17; licence for Certifying Authorities (S.21); the CCA's functions (S.18) include licensing and supervising CAs and laying down standards; S.35 DSC issue; S.36 representations; S.37 suspension; S.38 revocation; S.39 notice of suspension/revocation; Chapters on penalties and adjudication follow.
Evidence link: S.65B IEA (now S.63 BSA with a certificate in the Schedule and hash value); Anvar P.V. (2014), Arjun Panditrao (2020), Pune Bar Association (2026) - see Part 5.

topics.title: IT Act Offences and Penalties (S.43-78)
topics.summary: The highest-yield Cyber Law content: the civil penalty in S.43, the criminal offences in S.65-74, their punishments, cognizability and compounding.
key_points: S.43 (civil liability, compensation, no monetary cap after 2008): unauthorised access, downloading/copying, introducing a virus or contaminant, damage, disruption, denial of access, assisting unauthorised access, charging services to another's account, destroying or altering information, stealing/concealing source code (S.43(a)-(j)). S.43A: a body corporate that is negligent in implementing reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data, causing wrongful loss or gain, must compensate; implemented through the 2011 SPDI Rules; S.43A is to be omitted when S.44(2) DPDP Act commences (phased, expected May 2027 - verify).
S.65: tampering with computer source documents - up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both.
S.66: computer-related offences (dishonest or fraudulent doing of S.43 acts, i.e. hacking) - up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh or both.

S.66A (2008): sending offensive, false or annoying messages - up to 3 years and fine; struck down by Shreya Singhal v Union of India (24 March 2015) as vague, over-broad and violative of Art 19(1)(a), not saved by Art 19(2).

S.66B: dishonestly receiving a stolen computer resource - up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 1 lakh or both. S.66C: identity theft (fraudulent use of electronic signature, password or unique identification feature) - up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh. S.66D: cheating by personation using a computer resource - up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh.

S.66E: violation of privacy - capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area of a person without consent - up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both. S.66F: cyber terrorism (threatening unity, integrity, security or sovereignty or striking terror by denial of access, unauthorised access or introduction of contaminant, causing death/injury, damage or affecting critical information infrastructure) - imprisonment which may extend to life imprisonment.

S.67: publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form - first conviction up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh; second or subsequent up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh. S.67A: sexually explicit act or conduct - up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh (first); up to 7 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh (subsequent). S.67B: child pornography (publishing, transmitting, creating, browsing, enticing children, recording abuse) - up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh (first); up to 7 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh (subsequent). S.67C: intermediaries must preserve and retain information as prescribed (contravention up to 3 years and fine).

S.68: Controller's directions to certifying authorities (non-compliance up to 2 years or fine up to Rs 1 lakh). S.69: power to intercept, monitor or decrypt any information in the interest of sovereignty, security, public order or investigation of an offence - non-compliance up to 7 years and fine; Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Interception, Monitoring and Decryption of Information) Rules 2009. S.69A: power to direct blocking of public access - non-compliance up to 7 years and fine; Blocking Rules 2009; S.69A and the Rules were upheld in Shreya Singhal. S.69B: monitoring and collecting traffic data for cyber security - non-compliance up to 3 years and fine.

S.70: protected system - unauthorised access punishable up to 10 years and fine; S.70A: National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC); S.70B: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) as the national agency for incident response.

S.71: misrepresentation to the Controller; S.72: breach of confidentiality and privacy by a person who obtained information under the Act's powers - up to 2 years or fine up to Rs 1 lakh or both; S.72A (2008): disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract - up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh or both; S.73: publishing a false Digital Signature Certificate - up to 2 years or fine up to Rs 1 lakh; S.74: publication for fraudulent purpose - up to 2 years or fine up to Rs 1 lakh.

S.75: extra-territorial application; S.76: confiscation; S.77: compensation and penalties do not bar other punishments; S.77A: compounding of offences (by a court of competent jurisdiction) - not available for offences with imprisonment of more than 3 years, offences against a woman or child, or where the accused has a previous conviction or enhanced punishment; S.77B: offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 years and above are cognizable; offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 years are bailable; S.78: investigation by a police officer not below the rank of Inspector; S.80: any police officer not below the rank of Inspector (or other officer authorised by the Government) may enter, search and arrest without warrant in a public place.

S.84A (modes or methods for encryption), S.84B (abetment - same punishment as the offence) and S.84C (attempt - up to half of the longest term). S.85: offences by companies (persons in charge liable). S.81: overriding effect; the proviso says nothing restricts exercise of rights under the Copyright Act 1957 or Patents Act 1970.

Special law prevails: Sharat Babu Digumarti v Government of NCT of Delhi (2016) - where S.67 IT Act specifically covers an offence of obscene electronic material, the general S.292 IPC (S.294 BNS) is not attracted and the intermediary protected by S.79 is not prosecutable under IPC; State of Tamil Nadu v Suhas Katti (2004) - first conviction for obscene messages online (S.67 plus IPC S.469, 509). Even after Shreya Singhal, S.66A continued to be invoked; the Supreme Court in PUCL v Union of India (2021 order) directed states to stop prosecutions under it.

topics.title: Intermediary Liability, Safe Harbour (S.79), IT Rules 2021 and the 2026 Synthetic Content Amendment
topics.summary: S.79 protects intermediaries conditionally; Shreya Singhal read down 'actual knowledge'; the 2021 Rules impose due diligence and grievance duties, and the February 2026 amendment adds labelling and fast takedown for AI-generated (synthetic) content.
key_points: S.79(1)-(2): an intermediary is not liable for third-party information, data or communication link hosted or made available by it if (a) its function is limited to providing access to a communication system, or (b) it does not initiate the transmission, select the receiver or select or modify the information, and (c) it observes due diligence and other guidelines prescribed by the Central Government.

S.79(3): safe harbour is lost if (a) the intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided or induced the commission of the unlawful act, or (b) upon receiving actual knowledge, or on being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency, that information is being used to commit an unlawful act, it fails to expeditiously remove or disable access without vitiating the evidence. Shreya Singhal (2015) read down S.79(3)(b): 'actual knowledge' means knowledge through a court order or a notification by the appropriate Government (and the unlawful act must relate to Art 19(2)); intermediaries need not judge the legality of each request.

Case law on intermediaries: Avnish Bajaj v State (NCT of Delhi) (2008, Delhi HC) - Bazee.com CEO prosecution for obscene listing led to the 2008 amendments and the reformed S.79; Digumarti (2016) - special law; MySpace Inc v Super Cassettes Industries (Delhi HC DB, 2016) and Christian Louboutin SAS v Nakul Bajaj (Delhi HC, 2018) - an intermediary playing an active role (curating, promoting) can lose the safe harbour; Google India v Visakha Industries (2019) - intermediary liability in defamation context.

Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021: due diligence by intermediaries (user agreements; remove unlawful content on court order or government notice within 36 hours (now shortened - see below); retain data 180 days; assist agencies within 72 hours); Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs: 5 million or more registered users) must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, a Nodal Contact Person and a Resident Grievance Officer (all residents in India), publish monthly compliance reports, and messaging services must enable identification of the first originator of a message for serious offences (Rule 4(2); under challenge in WhatsApp v Union of India, Delhi HC). Grievance mechanism: acknowledge within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days (now 7 days); Part III covers digital news and OTT content - three-tier self-regulation. Online gaming intermediaries were added by IT Amendment Rules 2023 (self-regulatory bodies).

IT Amendment Rules 2026 on 'synthetically generated information' (SGI) (notified 10 February 2026, in force 20 February 2026): SGI is audio, visual or audio-visual content created or altered by a computer resource so that it appears authentic (deepfakes, voice cloning, AI-altered images; plain AI text is excluded). Lawful SGI must be clearly and prominently labelled; where feasible, intermediaries embed permanent metadata or unique identifiers; labels cannot be removed; the draft's 10% watermark was dropped. Timelines: unlawful content after a court order or government notice - 3 hours (earlier 36); content about an individual - 36 hours (earlier 72); high-risk content such as non-consensual intimate imagery, impersonation or morphed images - 2 hours (earlier 24); general grievances - 7 days (earlier 15). Failure of due diligence can cost safe harbour (reported; verify the final text).

Blocking: S.69A and the Blocking Rules 2009 (written reasons, committee review, hearing to the originator/intermediary where identifiable); emergency blocking; Sahyog portal for notices - X Corp v Union of India (Karnataka HC, September 2025) rejected X's challenge to the Sahyog portal; appeal reported - verify.

Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) is the nodal ministry; the proposed Digital India Act to replace the IT Act has not been enacted (verify). Telecommunications Act 2023 replaces the Indian Telegraph Act 1885 (interception, suspension of services, SIM-fraud offences) - being brought into force in phases (verify).

Internet shutdowns: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020) - freedom of speech and trade over the internet is protected by Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); indefinite shutdown impermissible; orders must be published, proportionate and reviewable; the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services Rules 2017 provide a Review Committee. Faheema Shirin v State of Kerala (Kerala HC, 2019): access to the internet is part of Art 21.

provisions.ref: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021; Amendment Rules 2026
provisions.note: Due diligence, SSMI duties, SGI labelling, takedown timelines.
