topics.title: Privacy and Data Protection - Puttaswamy, SPDI Rules 2011, DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025
topics.summary: Privacy is a fundamental right (Puttaswamy, 2017). India's first comprehensive data protection law is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, operationalised through the DPDP Rules 2025 in phases to about May 2027.
key_points: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (24 August 2017, 9 judges): right to privacy is a fundamental right under Art 21 and Part III; M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) overruled to the extent inconsistent. Any restriction must satisfy a three-fold test: legality (a law), legitimate aim and proportionality (rational nexus, necessity, minimal impairment). Informational privacy and the right to be left alone recognised. Puttaswamy II (26 September 2018): Aadhaar Act upheld by 4:1 but S.57 (private use) and S.33(2) struck down; Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for bank accounts and mobile connections. Earlier: PUCL v Union of India (1997) - telephone tapping guidelines; Kharak Singh and R. Rajagopal v State of T.N. (1994) - privacy and press.

Right to be forgotten and personality rights: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy recognised the idea; High Courts (Delhi, Karnataka, Orissa, Kerala) have ordered removal or anonymisation in specific cases (Zulfiqar Ahman Khan v Quintillion Business Media, Delhi HC 2019; Subhranshu Rout v State of Odisha, Orissa HC 2020); in 2025 the Delhi and Bombay High Courts granted personality-rights injunctions against AI-generated misuse of celebrities' voice and likeness (verify).

Pre-DPDP regime: S.43A IT Act and the IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011 (SPDI Rules): sensitive personal data includes passwords, financial information, health, sexual orientation, medical records and biometrics; body corporate must have a privacy policy, obtain written consent, allow review and correction, appoint a grievance officer, and implement ISO 27001 or equivalent security. S.72A penalises disclosure in breach of a lawful contract.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (assent 11 August 2023): applies to processing of digital personal data within India (and of non-digital data that is digitised) and to processing outside India in connection with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India (S.3). It does not apply to personal data processed for personal or domestic purposes, or to data made publicly available by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation. Definitions: Data Principal (the individual; includes parent or guardian of a child and lawful guardian of a person with disability), Data Fiduciary (determines purpose and means), Data Processor, Consent Manager, Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF), Child (below 18).

Grounds for processing: consent or certain 'legitimate uses' (S.4). Consent (S.6) must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, limited to the specified purpose, and as easy to withdraw as to give; a notice (S.5) in plain language, in English or any Eighth Schedule language, must precede the request. Legitimate uses (S.7): voluntary provision of data, State subsidies/benefits/licences, legal obligation, judicial orders, medical emergency, epidemics, disasters, employment purposes. S.6(9) Consent Managers (registered with the Board).

Obligations of Data Fiduciaries (S.8): accuracy, reasonable security safeguards, breach intimation to the Board and affected Data Principals, erasure when purpose is served or consent withdrawn, publication of contact details of a Data Protection Officer or person answering questions, grievance redressal. Children (S.9): verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian; no processing likely to cause detrimental effect; no tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children. Significant Data Fiduciary (S.10): notified by the Government (volume, sensitivity, risk to rights, security of State); duties - Data Protection Officer in India, independent data auditor, periodic Data Protection Impact Assessment.

Rights of Data Principals (S.11-14): access to a summary of personal data and processing; correction, completion, updating and erasure; grievance redressal; nomination of another person in case of death or incapacity. Duties (S.15): comply with laws, no impersonation, no false or frivolous complaints. No right to compensation is conferred by the Act.

Cross-border transfer (S.16): permitted except to countries or territories restricted by notification of the Central Government (a negative-list model); sectoral laws with stricter localisation prevail. Exemptions (S.17): State instrumentalities for sovereignty, security and public order (by notification); research, archiving and statistics; startups (notified classes); legal rights enforcement; courts; prevention of offences; contracts with foreign persons (processing by Indian outsourcing companies).

Data Protection Board of India (S.18-26): an independent adjudicatory body (a body corporate; chairperson and members appointed by the Central Government, with a head office in the National Capital Region as per the Rules; four members at inception); powers of civil court; inquiry on complaints, references, breach, orders to remedy, penalties; voluntary undertakings (S.31); mediation (S.30); appeals to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) (S.29); civil courts' jurisdiction barred (S.39).

Penalties (Schedule, S.33): failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach - up to Rs 250 crore; failure to give breach notice to the Board and Data Principals - up to Rs 200 crore; breach of obligations regarding children - up to Rs 200 crore; breach of SDF obligations - up to Rs 150 crore; breach of Data Principal's duties - up to Rs 10,000; breach of voluntary undertaking - up to the applicable amount; residuary - up to Rs 50 crore.

DPDP Rules 2025: notified 13 November 2025 with phased commencement - (i) 13 November 2025: Board constitution and administrative provisions (Rules 1-2, 17-21; Act S.1(2), 2, 18-26, 35, 38-43, 44(1) and (3)); (ii) after one year (about 12-13 November 2026): consent manager registration (S.6(9), S.27(1)(d); Rule 4); (iii) after 18 months (about 12 May 2027): all remaining provisions - notice and consent, fiduciary obligations, children's data, rights of Data Principals, cross-border rules and the Board's remaining powers (as reported; verify against the notification). Note that S.44(3) (amendment of S.8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, exempting personal information) is in the first tranche per the commencement list, whereas S.44(2) (omission of S.43A IT Act) falls in the last - verify. Rules also deal with breach reporting (immediately and a detailed report within 72 hours), verifiable parental consent, data retention periods for large platforms and SDF audits (verify details).

Interplay with other laws: S.38 DPDP - the Act is in addition to other laws; in conflict, the DPDP provision prevails to the extent of the inconsistency; sector laws on localisation (RBI payment data rules) continue. Aadhaar Act 2016 (S.8, 29, 33) and Right to Information Act (S.8(1)(j)) interplay noted.

topics.title: Authorities, Adjudication, Jurisdiction and Cyber Investigation Procedure
topics.summary: Who regulates and who decides: Controller of Certifying Authorities, Adjudicating Officer, TDSAT, CERT-In, NCIIPC, police and BNSS procedure for electronic evidence.
key_points: Adjudication (S.46): the Adjudicating Officer (an officer not below the rank of Director in the Central Government or equivalent in a State; in practice the Secretary of the IT department of the State) decides civil contraventions of Chapter IX (S.43-45) where the claim for injury or damage does not exceed Rs 5 crore; claims above that go to the competent civil court. S.47: factors for quantum (unfair advantage, loss, repeat). S.45: residuary penalty - compensation up to Rs 25,000 or penalty up to Rs 25,000.

Appeals: the Cyber Appellate Tribunal (S.48) was merged into the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) under the Finance Act 2017 and Tribunal reforms; appeal to the High Court within 60 days on a question of fact or law (S.62). S.61: civil court has no jurisdiction over matters within the Adjudicating Officer's or Tribunal's powers.

Controller of Certifying Authorities (S.17-18): licensing and supervising CAs; Root Certifying Authority of India (RCAI); CAs issue DSCs. CERT-In (S.70B): national agency for cyber security incidents; CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 require reporting of specified incidents within 6 hours, maintaining logs for 180 days within India and synchronising system clocks with NIC/NPL servers; VPN providers, data centres and cloud providers retain subscriber information for 5 years. NCIIPC (S.70A): protection of critical information infrastructure; S.70 protected systems.

Investigation: S.78 Inspector-rank police; S.80 search and arrest without warrant in public place by Inspector rank or authorised officer; BNSS 2023 provisions: S.94 (summons to produce documents/things including electronic communication devices), S.105 (audio-video recording of search and seizure), S.173 (e-FIR and Zero FIR), S.530 (trials, inquiries and proceedings by electronic means); evidence by Section 63 BSA certificate (hash value) - see Part 5. National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in), helpline 1930 and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Jurisdiction on the internet: IT Act S.75 (extra-territorial); Casio India v Ashita Tele Systems (Delhi HC, 2003) and Banyan Tree Holding v A. Murali Krishna Reddy (Delhi HC, 2010) - mere accessibility of a website is not enough; 'purposeful availment' and targeting are required for jurisdiction; domain names: Satyam Infoway Ltd v Sifynet Solutions (SC, 2004) - domain names are business identifiers; passing-off applies; Yahoo! Inc v Akash Arora (Delhi HC, 1999).
Cyber-crime and companies: S.85 (offences by companies); Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels (2012): directors can be prosecuted only if the company is arraigned.

Mutual legal assistance and cross-border data: India is not a party to the Budapest Convention; it has participated in negotiations on the UN Convention against Cybercrime (adopted by the UN General Assembly in December 2024; opened for signature in 2025) - verify India's position.

topics.title: Cyber Crimes under BNS and Emerging Issues - Deepfakes, Online Gaming, Digital Arrest, Cyber Fraud
topics.summary: Many cyber-crimes are prosecuted under both the IT Act and the BNS. Current trends: AI deepfakes, the online gaming ban, digital arrest scams and personality-rights litigation.
key_points: BNS equivalents (verify numbering): S.318 cheating (IPC 420), S.319 cheating by personation, S.336 forgery (includes electronic record), S.303 theft, S.356 defamation, S.351 criminal intimidation, S.75 sexual harassment (IPC 354A), S.77 voyeurism (IPC 354C - includes capture or dissemination of private images), S.78 stalking (IPC 354D - includes monitoring electronic communication), S.79 insulting the modesty of a woman, S.294 obscene material (IPC 292), S.196 promoting enmity through electronic communication, S.152 acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity (replaces sedition; electronic communication included), S.111 organised crime (includes cyber-crime) and S.113 terrorist act. 'Document' in BNS includes electronic and digital records. Where both the IT Act and IPC/BNS apply to the same act, Digumarti holds that a special law (IT Act) prevails for the subject it covers.

Deepfakes and AI: the 2026 IT Rules amendment on synthetically generated information (labelling, metadata and 2-3 hour takedowns); S.66C/66D (impersonation), S.66E, S.67/67A (sexual content), BNS defamation and cheating; personality-rights injunctions by the Delhi and Bombay High Courts in 2025 (verify).

Online gaming: the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 (assent 22 August 2025) prohibits online money games and their advertising and facilitation, establishes an authority for e-sports and social gaming promotion, and prescribes imprisonment and fines (reported up to 3 years and Rs 1 crore for offering; lower for advertising). Challenges are before the Supreme Court (verify). Earlier IT Amendment Rules 2023 created self-regulatory bodies for online gaming; GST rate hikes on online gaming (2023-2025) are a separate issue.

Digital arrest scams: fraudsters impersonate law-enforcement officers (CBI, police, customs) and extract money by 'virtual arrest'; the Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance in 2025 and directed coordination and a central probe (verify); the Government has issued advisories. Prosecuted under S.318/319 BNS, S.66C/66D IT Act and extortion provisions. 'Digital arrest' is not a recognised legal procedure.

Cyber fraud and banking: RBI's customer-liability circular (zero liability for third-party breach reported within 3 working days); UPI frauds; SIM-swap; phishing; vishing; sextortion. The Telecommunications Act 2023 introduces penalties for SIM-fraud and identity-based offences (verify provisions in force).
Cyber stalking, revenge porn and NCII: S.66E, S.67, S.67A, BNS S.77-78; StopNCII; the Delhi High Court's orders for takedown within defined time (Mrs X v Union of India, 2023).
E-commerce and consumer: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 and the 2023 Guidelines on Dark Patterns (CCPA) - see Part 8.
Critical infrastructure and national security: S.66F, S.70, S.70A; the National Cyber Security Policy 2013; the Digital India Act is proposed but not enacted (verify).

mcqs.q: The Information Technology Act 2000 is based on the Model Law on Electronic Commerce adopted by:
mcqs.explain: UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce, 1996 (General Assembly Resolution 51/162).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT excluded from the IT Act by the First Schedule?
mcqs.explain: Negotiable instruments other than a cheque are excluded; a cheque is not.

mcqs.q: Which section of the IT Act was struck down in Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015)?
mcqs.explain: S.66A violated Art 19(1)(a) and was not saved by Art 19(2).

mcqs.q: Identity theft is punishable under which section of the IT Act?
mcqs.explain: S.66C: up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh. S.66D is cheating by personation.

options: Imprisonment which may extend to life

options: 5 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh

7 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh
mcqs.explain: 7 years on subsequent conviction.

mcqs.q: S.66E of the IT Act punishes:
options: Violation of privacy by capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area
mcqs.explain: Up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both.

mcqs.q: The power to direct blocking of public access to information is contained in:
mcqs.explain: S.69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules; upheld in Shreya Singhal.

mcqs.explain: 5 million registered users in India.

mcqs.q: The Adjudicating Officer under S.46 IT Act can decide claims not exceeding:
mcqs.explain: Claims above Rs 5 crore lie before the competent civil court.

options: TDSAT (which absorbed the Cyber Appellate Tribunal)
mcqs.explain: Finance Act 2017 merged the CAT with TDSAT; then High Court within 60 days (S.62).

mcqs.q: Offences under the IT Act punishable with imprisonment of three years are:
mcqs.explain: S.77B: three years and above are cognizable; offences punishable with three years are bailable.

mcqs.q: An investigation of an offence under the IT Act can be carried out by a police officer not below the rank of:
mcqs.explain: S.78 IT Act.

options: A fundamental right under Art 21 and Part III
mcqs.explain: Nine-judge bench; test of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.

mcqs.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a 'child' is a person below the age of:
mcqs.explain: 18 years; verifiable parental consent and no tracking or targeted advertising.

mcqs.q: The maximum monetary penalty under the DPDP Act 2023 (Schedule) is:
mcqs.explain: For failure to take reasonable security safeguards.

mcqs.q: Appeal against an order of the Data Protection Board of India lies to:
mcqs.explain: S.29 DPDP Act.

mcqs.q: The DPDP Rules 2025 were notified on:
mcqs.explain: Phased commencement over about 18 months.

mcqs.q: In Sharat Babu Digumarti v Government of NCT of Delhi (2016), the Supreme Court held that:
options: IPC prevails over the IT Act
Where the IT Act covers the offence (S.67), the general IPC provision (S.292) is not attracted
mcqs.explain: Special law prevails over general law.

mcqs.q: In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020) the Supreme Court held that:
options: Freedom of speech and trade over the internet is protected and indefinite shutdowns are impermissible
The internet is not covered by Art 19
Only the Centre can suspend the internet
mcqs.explain: Orders must be proportionate, published and reviewable.

mcqs.q: Under the 2026 amendment to the IT Rules, unlawful content must be taken down within how many hours of a court order or government notice?
mcqs.explain: Earlier 36 hours; 2 hours for high-risk content such as NCII.

mcqs.q: In the First Schedule, which of the following is excluded from the IT Act?
options: A contract for sale or conveyance of immovable property
mcqs.explain: Immovable property contracts are excluded.

mcqs.q: Which section makes e-contracts enforceable despite being formed electronically?
mcqs.explain: S.10A inserted in 2008.

mcqs.q: The national agency for cyber security incident response under S.70B is:
mcqs.explain: NCIIPC (S.70A) protects critical information infrastructure.
